subject: zoology_2
question_text: What are multiple alleles? Describe multiple alleles with the help of ABO blood groups in man.

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.20, LAQ 6. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: What multiple alleles are
steps.why: A gene normally comes in two forms; when a population carries more than two forms of the same gene they are called multiple alleles.
common_mistakes: Saying one person carries three alleles. Each person carries two.
Confusing multiple alleles with multiple genes.
steps.memory_tip: More than two alleles of ONE gene in the population.
steps.margin_note: Definition, then the example, then the formula.
lines: Generally a gene has two alleles, one
dominant and the other recessive.
Sometimes a gene may have more than two
alleles. These are called multiple alleles.
Example: the ABO blood groups.

steps.label: The number of genotypes
steps.why: Each person carries two of the available alleles, and the formula simply counts every pair that can be made from n alleles.
common_mistakes: Writing the formula without substituting n = 3.
steps.memory_tip: n(n+1)/2 — with three alleles that is 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6.
steps.margin_note: Substitute the numbers. The working carries the mark.
lines: The number of genotypes for multiple
alleles is given by:
where n is the number of alleles.
For ABO blood groups there are 3 alleles.

steps.label: The four blood groups
steps.why: The group is decided by which sugar antigens sit on the red cell surface, so naming the antigen names the group.
common_mistakes: Saying the antigens are proteins. They are sugar polymers.
Placing the antigens in the plasma. They are on the red cells.
steps.memory_tip: Antigens on the cell, antibodies in the plasma.
steps.margin_note: Name the four groups before describing them.
lines: The four blood groups A, B, AB and O are
decided by the presence or absence of
antigens on the plasma membrane of the red
blood cells.
The antigens are sugar polymers bound to
lipid molecules.

steps.label: Antigens and antibodies
steps.why: A person never carries the antibody against their own antigen, or their own blood would be destroyed.
common_mistakes: Giving group AB both antibodies. It has none.
Giving group O antigens. It has none.
steps.memory_tip: AB has both antigens and no antibodies; O has no antigens and both antibodies.
steps.margin_note: Four lines, one per group. Keep the pattern visible.
lines: Group A has antigen A on the red cells and
anti-B antibodies in the plasma.
Group B has antigen B and anti-A
antibodies.
Group AB has antigens A and B, and no
anti-A or anti-B antibodies.
Group O has no antigens, and both anti-A
and anti-B antibodies.

steps.label: The three alleles
steps.why: All three alleles sit at the same place on chromosome 9, which is what makes them alleles of one gene rather than three genes.
common_mistakes: Placing the gene on the wrong chromosome. It is chromosome 9.
Giving Iᴼ an antigen. It produces none.
steps.memory_tip: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᴼ — one gene, chromosome 9.
steps.margin_note: Name the proposer and the chromosome. Both are marked.
lines: Karl Landsteiner proposed the ABO system
of blood groups.
The genetic basis depends on three alleles
of the gene I on chromosome 9.

lines.text: The alleles are Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᴼ (or i)

lines: Iᴬ produces antigen A and Iᴮ produces
antigen B. Iᴼ produces no antigen.

steps.label: Dominance between them
steps.why: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, so a person carrying both shows both antigens instead of only one.
common_mistakes: Calling Iᴬ dominant over Iᴮ. They are codominant.
Leaving out that both are dominant over Iᴼ.
steps.memory_tip: Both beat Iᴼ, but neither beats the other.
steps.margin_note: One line, but it explains the AB group.
lines: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant over Iᴼ, but they
are codominant to each other.
A child receives one of the three alleles
from each parent.

steps.label: Six genotypes, four phenotypes
steps.why: Six pairs are possible but two pairs give the same visible group, so six genotypes collapse into four phenotypes.
common_mistakes: Giving six phenotypes. There are four.
Missing IᴬIᴼ or IᴮIᴼ from the list.
steps.memory_tip: Six pairs, four groups: the two Iᴼ pairs hide inside A and B.
steps.margin_note: List all six, then group them into four.
lines: The 6 genotypes are:

lines.text: IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴮ, IᴮIᴼ, IᴬIᴮ, IᴼIᴼ

lines: The 4 phenotypes are:
IᴬIᴬ and IᴬIᴼ give group A.
IᴮIᴮ and IᴮIᴼ give group B.
IᴬIᴮ gives group AB.
IᴼIᴼ gives group O.

steps.label: Donor and recipient
steps.why: A group with no antigens cannot be attacked by any antibody, and a group with no antibodies cannot attack any donor cell.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two. O negative donates to all; AB positive receives from all.
steps.memory_tip: O⁻ gives to everyone; AB⁺ takes from everyone.
steps.margin_note: Close with the two special groups.
lines: AB⁺ can receive blood from all the other
groups, so it is the universal recipient.
O⁻ can be given to any other group, but can
receive only from O⁻.

lines.text: So O⁻ is called the universal donor

insider_note: Show the n(n+1)/2 working with numbers substituted. Writing only '6 genotypes' loses the mark that the formula carries.
